newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Riksbank says inflation pressure still weak.
newsitem.headline: Riksbank says inflation pressure still weak.

text.p: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, said on Thursday there could be further room to lower its key interest rate, the repo rate, and noted stronger signs of economic recovery during the autumn.
It said Sweden's low inflation climate was continuing and inflation could end below one percent for the full year 1996.
In an address to a public hearing with the government finance committee, Riksbank governor Urban Backstrom commented on the central bank's monetary policy over the past year.
The central bank recently pegged its key repo rate at 4.60 percent for four of its consecutive weekly reverse repurchase operations, bringing it into line with Bundesbank practice.
Previously the bank had been cutting the repo rate every other week.

"The motive for our actions is that while we see some limited room for further cuts in the repo rate, the scenario is not unambiguous. We need time to analyse and follow statistics that come in," the bank said.
The conclusion of this analysis could be that the repo rate is left unchanged, Backstrom said.

A nascent recovery in the Swedish economy could make the central bank less inclined to make further reductions to the repo rate, which has fallen to 4.60 percent from 8.91 percent at the start of the year.

"After the summer and during the autumn, we have seen clearer signs of an improved economy. The conditions for further improvements in growth over the coming two years also seem to be favourable," he said.

Even so, inflationary pressure in the economy was firmly under control, and there was a chance that inflation would remain below the lower tolerance limit of the bank's one to three percent inflation target.
"Looking at 1996 as a whole, we cannot rule out the possibility that inflation may remain slightly below the lower (one percent) tolerance limit," Backstrom said.
This reduced inflation propensity and the relative weakness of the export sector could help restrict wage rises in the future, he said.
"If this hypothesis is reasonable, we should expect a gradual reduction in the rate of wage increases as existing wage agreements come to an end," Backstrom said.
The central bank has recently emphasised the importance of keeping wage rises under control in the battle against inflation.
